To rave means to express something in an intense, unrestrained way — either with wild excitement and praise, or with wild anger and madness. In both cases, the person is going well beyond calm, controlled expression. That feeling of losing yourself in the intensity of what you're saying is what unifies this word.
Sense 1 — To talk about something with enormous enthusiasm and admiration

This is the most common everyday meaning. When you rave about something, you praise it so strongly and excitedly that your words pour out almost uncontrollably — you can't stop talking about how wonderful it is.

Examples:

  • "She raved about the restaurant for days after visiting."
  • "Critics raved about the film."
  • "He kept raving about how beautiful the mountains were."

A few things to notice here:

"About" almost always follows. You rave about something. That's the standard pattern.

The praise is extreme, not mild. If you rave about a book, you don't just say "it was good." You are expressing admiration at full volume — gushing, enthusiastic, hard to contain.

It can sound slightly over the top, but not in a dishonest way. It means the person is genuinely swept away by how much they liked something.
Sense 2 — To speak wildly, incoherently, or furiously

This is an older and more serious meaning. In this sense, to rave is to speak in a way that is out of control — because of illness, madness, or extreme anger. The speech is disorganized, loud, irrational, or impossible to reason with.

Examples:

  • "The sick man raved through the night in his fever."
  • "She raved at him for an hour without making any sense."
  • "The old man raved about the end of the world to anyone who would listen."

This sense is associated with:

  • Delirium or fever — a sick person talking nonsense because their mind is clouded
  • Mental breakdown — someone losing grip on reality
  • Extreme, uncontrolled anger — someone so furious they are beyond reason

Notice: in this sense, "rave" doesn't need "about." You can rave at someone, or just rave without any preposition.
How to tell the two senses apart

The context tells you everything:

SituationSense

If someone is raving in a happy, excited, positive situation — talking about food, movies, a trip, a person they admire — it's almost certainly Sense 1 (wild enthusiasm and praise).

If someone is raving in a context of illness, madness, distress, or fury — it's almost certainly Sense 2 (wild, irrational speech).

Sometimes they blend. If someone praises something with such extreme excitement that they seem almost out of their mind with enthusiasm, both senses are subtly present — and that overlap is actually part of the word's personality.

1. Rave reviews
One of the most common phrases in English. It means overwhelmingly positive critical responses. Here "rave" functions as an adjective (coming from Sense 1).

  • "The play opened to rave reviews."
  • "Her debut novel received rave reviews from critics."

This phrase shows up constantly in journalism, entertainment, and everyday speech.

2. Rant and rave
A very natural pairing. To rant and rave means to shout, complain, and carry on angrily for a long time — in a way that is exhausting, excessive, and out of proportion.

  • "He ranted and raved but no one took him seriously."
  • "There's no point ranting and raving about things you can't change."

Rant = to speak angrily at length. Rave = to do so in a wild, irrational, uncontrolled way. Together, they paint a picture of someone completely losing their composure.

3. Raving mad / a raving lunatic
Here "raving" is used as an intensifying adjective. It means completely and obviously insane or irrational — mad in a loud, wild, impossible-to-ignore way.

  • "By the end of the ordeal, he was raving mad."
  • "You'd have to be a raving lunatic to agree to that."

It's often used hyperbolically (for humor or exaggeration), not literally.

4. Raving about someone
In casual speech, especially when someone is deeply attracted to another person, you might hear:

  • "She's been raving about him since they met."

This is just Sense 1 applied to a person — expressing extreme admiration.

Rave always carries a sense of intensity that has broken free from its container. Whether the emotion is joy and admiration (Sense 1) or anger and madness (Sense 2), the person raving is not speaking in a measured, calm, or moderate way. They have crossed into territory that is louder, more emotional, and more unrestrained than everyday speech.

This is why "rave reviews" feel more powerful than "good reviews," and why "rant and rave" sounds more alarming than "complain." The word stretches language toward its edges.

• Rave = to express something intensely and without restraint
  • Positive context → enthusiastic, gushing praise (rave about the food)
  • Negative/distressed context → wild, irrational, or furious speech (rave in a fever; rant and rave)
  • Key phrases: rave reviews, rant and rave, raving mad
